newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian army quits Chechnya but peace still shaky.
newsitem.headline: Russian army quits Chechnya but peace still shaky.

text.p: Just over two years after Russian tanks thundered into Chechnya in a three-pronged offensive to crush its secessionist leadership, the last Russian soldier has left the southern region, leaving the separatists in charge.
After tens of thousands of mostly civilian deaths, this weekend's final Russian pullout has, in one sense, restored the status quo that prevailed before the December 1994 offensive.

Yet the political terrain has been transformed by the war, which ended in humiliation for the Russian army but also destroyed much of Chechnya's industrial capacity and housing. The way ahead to preserve an uneasy peace is far from clear.

Under a truce hammered out after rebel guerrillas recaptured the Chechen capital Grozny in August, the crucial question of secession was left to one side, possibly for up to five years, in the interests of securing a military ceasefire.
But the two sides seem as far apart as ever and the issue will simply not go away, particularly in view of elections for a new Chechen president and local assembly due on January 27.
"It's very hard to forecast what will happen in the long term," said Viktor Kremenyuk, deputy head of a Moscow think-tank, the USA and Canada Institute.
"Necessarily, bilateral relations must be established that allow Moscow to save face and also satisfy the Chechens' desire for independence."

Some analysts believe President Boris Yeltsin, far from accepting a position of weakness, has freed his hand by finally acceding to rebel demands to remove the final units of Russian troops. They are no longer targets for attack or hostage-taking.

The Kremlin could withhold aid and investment for Chechnya's ravaged economy. Tycoon turned Security Council official Boris Berezovsky has concentrated peace efforts on building economic cooperation over reopening Chechnya's lucrative oil pipelines.
Moscow could even threaten new military strikes in its efforts to negotiate a face-saving settlement, Kremenyuk said.

It must show some success in maintaining its refusal to recognise Chechen sovereignty to avoid deepening disillusion in the army, which feels frustrated by its inability to annihilate Chechen resistance, and to discourage other ethnic groups across the sprawling federation from pressing for more autonomy.
Yet the winner of this month's presidential election, organised with Moscow's blessing, is certain to be committed, at least in public, to winning outright independence.

More than a dozen candidates are seeking the presidency, including Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev, whom the separatist rebels recognised as their leader following the death of the charismatic Dzhokhar Dudayev in a rocket attack last April.

Only five candidates, including Yandarbiyev and the supreme guerrilla commander Aslan Maskhadov, who negotiated the truce, are credited with much support among the one million population -- many of them now living as refugees outside Chechnya.

All of them have pledged to lead the region to independence. A blatant failure to deliver on that promise would be likely to spark violent reprisals from heavily armed hardliners, many of them partisans of consolidating Islamic law in the republic.

But, analysts say, none of the potential winners -- and especially Maskhadov, who is running as favourite -- will want to risk a new confrontation with Russia or the loss of badly needed investment which Moscow promises will follow the vote.
"Despite Moscow's military defeat and the withdrawal of troops, Moscow still has more room for manoeuvre, politically and economically, than the new Chechen leader," Kremenyuk said.
The new president in Grozny will have to tread a fine line between disappointing hardliners within Chechnya and pushing Moscow into retaliating, he concluded.
